questions.q: What does Oracle's Cost-Based Optimizer use to estimate the cost of candidate execution plans?
options: Optimizer statistics stored in the data dictionary, such as row counts, distinct values, and histograms
A fixed cost table that never changes regardless of the data
The exact wall-clock time of the last execution
Whatever the DBA manually types into the query hint
questions.explain: The CBO estimates cost from stored optimizer statistics describing the data — not from live computation or fixed values.

questions.q: What is the supported, modern way to gather Oracle optimizer statistics?
options: The DBMS_STATS package, e.g. DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATS
The legacy ANALYZE TABLE statement, which the CBO fully trusts in all modern releases
Statistics can only be gathered by restarting the instance
UPDATE STATISTICS, borrowed directly from SQL Server syntax
questions.explain: DBMS_STATS is the supported package for gathering optimizer statistics; ANALYZE TABLE is legacy for this purpose.

questions.q: Why does a histogram matter for a column like STATUS that is 95% one value?
options: It captures the skewed distribution that a simple average or uniform assumption would misrepresent
Histograms are purely cosmetic and don't affect plan choices
Histograms replace the need for row counts entirely
Oracle requires a histogram on every column or statistics gathering fails
questions.explain: Histograms give the CBO extra detail about skewed value distributions, which a simple average-based estimate would misrepresent.

questions.q: What does Oracle's automatic statistics-gathering job (Auto Optimizer Stats Collection) do by default?
options: Runs in the nightly maintenance window and refreshes statistics for tables with significant tracked changes
Gathers statistics continuously in real time after every single row change
Only runs once, at database creation
Is disabled by default in every Oracle edition
questions.explain: The task runs by default in the nightly maintenance window, using DBA_TAB_MODIFICATIONS to find tables that changed enough to warrant a refresh.

questions.q: After a batch job loads 5 million rows into a table that had 10,000 rows that morning, why shouldn't you just wait for the nightly stats job?
options: The next queries could run against badly stale statistics in the meantime, risking a fundamentally wrong plan, not just a slow one
The nightly job would delete the new rows
Waiting is always fine because Oracle statistics never go stale
DBMS_STATS can only be run once per day system-wide
questions.explain: Statistics that still describe the pre-load table can cause the CBO to choose a fundamentally wrong plan (like a nested loop sized for ten rows) until they're refreshed.
